Get the PDF now

Houston Air & Heating hands the book out because the questions in it come up on hot Houston afternoons, when an air conditioner has quit and a decision feels urgent. Below you will find what each part of the book covers, the main rules checked again against current EPA and IRS pages, and what they mean when a quote lands on your table.

The R-410A phase out, in the book's own order

The book's central point is that most articles blur three separate things: manufacturing a new unit, putting a unit into a house, and fixing the one already there. The rules treat each one differently.

  • Building new equipmentNewly built home and light commercial cooling and heat pump systems must use a refrigerant whose global warming potential (GWP) is under the EPA's limit of 700. GWP compares how much heat a gas traps with the same amount of carbon dioxide. The book lists R-410A at 2,088, R-454B at 466 and R-32 at 675, which is why new systems moved to the last two.
  • Installing itAn EPA final rule signed in May 2026 removed the January 1, 2026 installation date for systems built entirely from components produced or brought into the country before 2025. That lets distributors keep selling and contractors keep installing older R-410A stock.
  • Servicing what you ownRepairing and recharging an installed system was not restricted by these rules. The book puts it simply: a failed compressor or coil can be replaced with an R-410A part.

A second, separate program comes from the AIM Act. Under it, the EPA is shrinking the supply of HFC refrigerants step by step until 2036, when it reaches 15 percent of the historic baseline. EPA's schedule holds at 60 percent of baseline from 2024 through 2028, then drops to 30 percent from 2029 through 2033, 20 percent in 2034 and 2035, and 15 percent from 2036 on. The book reads this as service prices that rise in jumps, with the 2029 step the one to watch, not as a date when repairs stop. It also notes that reclaimed refrigerant, recovered from old systems and cleaned, does not count against those limits.

One line in the book is worth knowing before any quote: when both the outdoor condenser and the indoor coil are swapped at once, EPA treats the job as a new installation, not a repair, and the new-equipment rules apply. Swapping one broken component is still a repair. Told that a part "can't be replaced anymore"? The book's advice is to ask exactly which part and on what basis.

What is inside, chapter by chapter

Its epigraph is a verse from Proverbs about hearing the other side before judging a case, and the whole book follows that habit: go to the rule itself, then test what others claim it says.

The rules (chapters 1 to 4, 14, 16)

How the 2026 installation deadline was set, softened and then removed; what the 700 GWP limit restricts and why R-454B and R-32 replaced R-410A; the stepped phasedown; and the outlook for R-410A supply for repairs. Chapter 16 covers what is still unsettled, including a court challenge, and how to check the EPA's own pages yourself.

The money (chapters 5, 6, 10, 19)

The reasons per-pound refrigerant figures online range so far apart (a wholesale price, a marked-up price and a price that folds in labor all get the same label), reported costs for new systems, the federal 25C credit ending, and what the SEER2, EER2 and HSPF2 numbers on a quote mean for your power bill.

The decision (chapters 7, 9, 12, 13, 21, 22)

Typical equipment lifespans and the signs that actually call for replacement, why a Manual J load calculation matters more than the refrigerant, treating a leak as the real problem, keeping a system healthy, why heat pumps keep coming up in quotes, and what to do when the AC dies in the middle of summer.

The people and the paperwork (chapters 8, 11, 15, 17, 18, 20)

R-454B versus R-32, choosing a contractor and spotting pressure tactics, buying or selling a house with an older system, a "what to do Monday morning" checklist, what the earlier R-22 phase out teaches, and ductwork. Appendices give a timeline, questions to ask in each situation, the published price figures side by side, and where to verify the rules.

Three ideas from the book that help with a Houston quote

Low refrigerant means a leak

The book's chapter on leaks starts from a simple fact: refrigerant circulates in a closed loop and is never consumed. If the charge is low, it escaped somewhere, and topping it up without finding the leak buys a few months at best. The question it suggests asking is where the leak is and whether it can be repaired so it lasts. The AC not cooling guide covers the safe checks to do first, starting with the air filter.

Sizing beats brand

An oversized system cools the air quickly and shuts off before it removes much moisture, which in a humid climate like Houston's leaves a house cool but clammy. The book urges homeowners to ask for a Manual J load calculation done in the house, to see the result, and to question a proposed size well above it. The AC installation page explains what a complete replacement quote should list.

Urgency is a signal

The final chapter speaks to the moment many Houston homeowners know well: the system fails in August and a large decision has to be made in a hot house. The book's advice is to get the failed part named and the diagnosis in writing, ask whether a repair will reliably get you through the season, and still ask for model numbers, a load calculation and the labor warranty before signing. It also notes that if seniors, small children or anyone heat sensitive is in the house, speed matters more than savings.

Checked against current rules

Because these rules have changed several times, the regulatory points on this page were checked again on October 8, 2026 against the sources listed below:

  • The EPA's sector table lists a 700 GWP limit for new home and light commercial cooling and heat pump systems.
  • An EPA final rule signed in May 2026 and published in the Federal Register that month removes the January 1, 2026 installation compliance date for equipment manufactured or imported before January 1, 2025; the EPA's regulatory actions page lists Technology Transitions rulemakings, and industry press covered the change.
  • The EPA says the AIM Act phases HFCs down to 15 percent of historic baseline levels by 2036, in steps.
  • Under EPA's Section 608 sales restriction, refrigerant for home systems can only be bought by certified technicians or their employers. Homeowners cannot buy it to recharge a system themselves.
  • The IRS says the section 25C Energy Efficient Home Improvement Credit is not allowed for property placed in service after December 31, 2025.

Cost figures in the book are reported as other sources published them, not as the book's own estimates, and they are national figures. Real quotes in Houston vary with the house, the equipment and the company. For what drives a local repair price, read the AC repair cost guide, and for the bigger choice, the repair or replace guide.

Common questions

Is the AC guide really free?

Yes. There is no charge and nothing to buy afterward. Save it, read it on any screen, or print it for your household. To pass it on, the book's front page asks readers to send people this web address instead of the file itself.

Will you ask for my email or phone number first?

Not at all. Tapping the button opens the file itself; you never see a sign-up box, an account screen or a mailing list. You only give your number if you decide to call the line about your own heating or cooling.

Is my R-410A air conditioner now illegal to keep?

No. The 700 GWP cap applies to newly made home cooling and heat pump equipment. It never forced owners to retire a working system, and an R-410A unit can still be repaired and recharged. A May 2026 EPA final rule also dropped the January 1, 2026 installation cutoff for equipment built or imported before 2025. Let the age, condition and repair bill decide when to replace, not a calendar date.

Can a technician switch my old system over to R-454B?

No, according to the book. Although the two run at close to the same pressures, they use different oils, R-454B carries the A2L rating (low toxicity, mildly flammable) with equipment rules to match, and components are certified for a single refrigerant. If anyone offers that conversion, the book says to turn it down.

Can I still claim the federal 25C tax credit on a new system?

Not for a 2026 installation. The IRS says the Energy Efficient Home Improvement Credit (section 25C) is not allowed for property placed in service after December 31, 2025. Utility or state programs may still exist, so ask about them and confirm any rebate a quote lists.

Who wrote the book?

Maurice Johnson. The book explains rules that changed fast, written for homeowners and home buyers. It is general reading; it cannot stand in for a technician inspecting your own equipment.
